newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sumitomo may file lawsuit against trader over loss.
newsitem.headline: Sumitomo may file lawsuit against trader over loss.

text.p: Sumitomo Corp may file a civil lawsuit against the copper trader blamed for causing $1.8 billion in losses to the giant Japanese trading house, sources close to the investigation said on Monday.

The Tokyo District Public Prosecutor's Office has already launched a probe into the huge losses, which Sumitomo has pinned on Yasuo Hamanaka for unauthorised copper trades over a decade, and is questioning other Sumitomo officials who had ties to Hamanaka.
Sumitomo and the prosecutor's office have been coordinating their investigations into the losses.
"The Tokyo prosecutor's office has already started questioning Sumitomo officials. It is collecting data before questioning Hamanaka himself," a source close to the prosecutor's office said.

The sources said last week the officials to be questioned by the Tokyo prosecutor's office include Masahiro Mogari, who worked as a senior copper trader until July, and Akio Imamura, general manager of Sumitomo's non-ferrous metals division.
They were not available for comment.
The authorities have also expressed a keen interest in Sumitomo's copper losses.
"We're aware of how significant the Sumitomo copper scandal is," said Nobuhisa Toda, a director of the Justice Ministry's Criminal Affairs bureau.
"And we've been in close contact with overseas authorities. I can't discuss the contents (of the discussions) in detail at the moment," the senior Justice Ministry official said.
Sumitomo, one of Japan's largest trading houses, announced on June 13 that Hamanaka had lost $1.8 billion in unauthorised copper trades, mainly on the London Metal Exchange, over a 10-year period.
It fired Hamanaka the next day and the former star trader has been in seclusion ever since.
U.S. and British law enforcement authorities have already opened investigations into the case to determine if any illegal trading practices were conducted in their countries.
Sumitomo said it could not disclose its plans amid an internal investigation into the copper losses, but did say it was considering charging Hamanaka with breach of trust.
"As long as our internal investigation is still taking place, we can't tell you the details. But filing a civil lawsuit is one of the options we can take," a Sumitomo spokesman said.
A source close to the investigation told Reuters that Sumitomo had already decided to file a civil lawsuit against Hamanaka, who has been closeted at home since the scandal broke.

Over the weekend, chaos erupted outside Hamanaka's home in a middle-class suburb of Tokyo as reporters and camera crews jostled for space, waiting for the former Sumitomo trader to emerge from his house.
"We have nothing to tell you all at the moment," Hamanaka's daughter said.
Little has been heard from Hamanaka since the scandal broke out, but the former trader told Reuters last month that he has been living a quiet life and had not been contacted by the company.
"I have been living in my home since leaving Sumitomo," Hamanaka said.
